A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of backdoored LLMs through model-generated explanations. All 14 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v3, including their appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original backdoor experiments, explanation-quality scores, similarity tests, and analyses of prediction trajectories and attention.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical analyses and adds human assessments, clean-model controls, poison-rate experiments, and evaluated backdoor detectors.

M1.justification: V1 leaves explanation-based detection as future work. V3 Section 6 introduces operational detection procedures: five-shot GPT-4o classification of explanation texts and supervised classifiers using layerwise maximum-token probabilities. These extend the retained explanation-analysis framework with a substantial new inference component.

E1.justification: V3 adds syntactic-trigger evaluation on SST-2, sentence-trigger evaluation on Twitter Emotion, and an actual poisoned-input detection task with cross-dataset and cross-trigger transfer tests. V1's flip-token scenario disappears. Sentiment classification and jailbreak generation remain covered; the PDFs do not establish whether renaming the generation dataset from BadNets to AdvBench represents different underlying data.

E2.justification: V3 Table 4 introduces a comparison among GPT-4o, logistic regression, SVM, decision tree, and random-forest detectors. V1 has no corresponding evaluated detector comparison. This adds a substantial set of comparison methods.

E3.justification: The LLaMA 2-13B configuration is removed, and DeepSeek-7B is introduced with its own training settings. V3 changes the token-level metric from MPC to MED and introduces human-rating, five-shot detection, and classifier evaluation protocols. Quality assessment changes from a stated 20-example GPT-4 subset to GPT-4o scoring of generated explanations. The reported generation-training mix also changes from 150 clean/200 poisoned samples to 200 clean/150 poisoned samples.

E4.justification: V3 adds independent human validation of explanation quality, a non-backdoored-model control, a 2% versus 9% poison-rate study, and detector transfer across datasets and triggers (Appendices B, D, J, and K). New aggregate layerwise and tokenwise plots supplement the retained example trajectories and attention analyses. These substantially expand validation and robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions generate five explanation variants per input and report t-tests for clean-versus-poisoned differences. V3 extends this practice to additional results but introduces no new confidence intervals, error bars, significance-testing procedure, training-run counts, or seed reporting. The human assessments do not report inter-rater uncertainty.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive quality, control, human-assessment, robustness, and detector results; Table 4 reports 97.5% accuracy for GPT-4o and 98.8% for logistic regression. It corrects the reported consistency finding to favor clean explanations. Table 1 changes SST-2 word-trigger ASR from 98% to 95%, although v3 Appendix A.1 still states 98%. Generation results are replaced under a changed reported training mix, so they do not establish a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: Equation 3 changes mathematically: v1's MPC averages token probabilities, whereas v3's MED averages layer-index-weighted probabilities. Appendix A.2 also adds asymptotic computational-cost estimates. The other lens, attention, and similarity definitions remain essentially unchanged; renaming lookback ratio as contextual reliance does not change its formula. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: A central headline finding reverses. V1's abstract, introduction, and Section 3.4 claim that poisoned-input explanations are more consistent; v3's abstract, introduction, and Section 4 describe them as more diverse and less consistent. The principal claims about delayed token emergence and reduced attention to input context remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of the new controls and transfer studies: trigger presence alone has relatively little effect on clean-model explanations, and detector transfer is attributed to recognizing irrational explanations rather than attack-specific overfitting. Appendix J proposes an explanation for poison-rate effects on clean-input scores. The limitations replace the earlier trigger/model restrictions with a new qualification about excluding self-explaining rationalization techniques.

D1.justification: V3 discloses complete quality-assessment and detector prompts, human-rating criteria, additional training settings, and generation-ASR assessment details. Appendix A.2 adds A100 hardware information and approximate training, explanation-generation, and lens-computation times. These substantially improve documentation, although v1's explicit QLoRA training disclosure is removed and detector training/test splits remain unspecified.

R1.justification: V3 adds literature on natural-language explanation uncertainty and self-rationalization, including Bills et al., Tanneru et al., and Liu et al., plus references for newly named models and data. It removes the mechanistic-circuit discussion and associated references. The central positioning of using LLM-generated explanations to investigate backdoors remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, explanation analysis, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. V3 organizes the introduction around two research questions, separates explanation analysis into its own section, and presents the internal-generation analysis through four explicit findings. The limitations and appendix organization are also substantially revised.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the workflow in Figure 2, adds quality and aggregate trajectory plots, introduces numerous structured evaluation tables, and displays complete prompts in boxed figures. Table 1 becomes a compact performance table, and explanation examples are reformatted. Several earlier heatmaps and prediction trajectories are retained with changed placement and numbering.

improvement.justification: V3 corrects v1's central consistency claim, bringing it into agreement with the earlier similarity plot and stated tests. Human assessments, clean-model controls, syntactic-trigger and poison-rate tests substantially strengthen the explanation-quality evidence, while evaluated detectors replace a speculative application. Full prompts and resource details also improve reproducibility. Important reporting problems remain: attack scores disagree between tables and Appendix A.1, and the new MED formula is not reconciled with Figure 7's plotted scale. These limit confidence in particular quantitative claims, but the gains in validation and clarity constitute a substantial overall improvement.
